claim: Vertebrate centrioles normally propagate through duplication.
source: Vertebrate centrioles normally propagate through duplication, but in the absence of preexisting centrioles, de novo synthesis can occur.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about centriole biology.

claim: In the absence of preexisting centrioles, de novo synthesis of centrioles can occur.
source: Vertebrate centrioles normally propagate through duplication, but in the absence of preexisting centrioles, de novo synthesis can occur.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript and established knowledge.

claim: Centriole formation is thought to strictly rely on self-assembly involving self-oligomerization of the centriolar protein SAS-6.
source: Consistently, centriole formation is thought to strictly rely on self-assembly, involving self-oligomerization of the centriolar protein SAS-6.
evidence: This represents the prevailing model in the field prior to this study.

claim: Normal looking centrioles capable of duplication and ciliation can arise in the absence of SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
source: Here, through reconstitution of de novo synthesis in human cells, we surprisingly found that normal looking centrioles capable of duplication and ciliation can arise in the absence of SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Canonically duplicated centrioles always form correctly.
source: Moreover, whereas canonically duplicated centrioles always form correctly, de novo centrioles are prone to structural errors, even in the presence of SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by EM data showing 100% accuracy in canonical duplication.

claim: De novo centrioles are prone to structural errors, even in the presence of SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
source: Moreover, whereas canonically duplicated centrioles always form correctly, de novo centrioles are prone to structural errors, even in the presence of SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by EM data showing structural defects in de novo centrioles.

claim: Centriole biogenesis does not strictly depend on SAS-6 self-assembly.
source: These results indicate that centriole biogenesis does not strictly depend on SAS-6 self-assembly, and may require preexisting centrioles to ensure structural accuracy, fundamentally deviating from the current paradigm.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental results showing centriole formation without SAS-6 self-oligomerization.

claim: Centriole biogenesis may require preexisting centrioles to ensure structural accuracy.
source: These results indicate that centriole biogenesis does not strictly depend on SAS-6 self-assembly, and may require preexisting centrioles to ensure structural accuracy, fundamentally deviating from the current paradigm.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that canonical duplication is error-free while de novo synthesis is error-prone.

claim: Centrioles are microtubule-based, ninefold symmetrical structures essential for centrosome and cilia formation.
source: Centrioles are microtubule-based, ninefold symmetrical structures essential for centrosome and cilia formation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about centriole structure and function.

claim: In cycling cells, centrioles are maintained in fixed numbers and formed through canonical duplication depending on pre-existing (or mother) centrioles.
source: In cycling cells, centrioles are maintained in fixed numbers, and formed through canonical duplication depending on pre-existing (or mother) centrioles.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about centriole biology.

claim: In the absence of pre-existing centrioles, de novo synthesis can occur.
source: In the absence of pre-existing centrioles, however, de novo synthesis can occur (Khodjakov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The number of centrioles formed through the de novo pathway is highly variable.
source: The number of centrioles formed through the de novo pathway is highly variable (Khodjakov et al., 2002; La Terra et al., 2005), providing an explanation for why canonical duplication dominates in dividing cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The variability in centriole number through de novo synthesis provides an explanation for why canonical duplication dominates in dividing cells.
source: The number of centrioles formed through the de novo pathway is highly variable (Khodjakov et al., 2002; La Terra et al., 2005), providing an explanation for why canonical duplication dominates in dividing cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited observations about de novo synthesis variability.

claim: In post-mitotic cells such as multi-ciliated epithelia, the genes required for centriole assembly are highly up-regulated.
source: In contrast to cycling cells, in post-mitotic cells such as multi-ciliated epithelia, the genes required for centriole assembly are highly up-regulated (Hoh et al., 2012) to produce large, variable numbers of centrioles prior to ciliogenesis, a process thought to primarily depend on de novo assembly (Dirksen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Multi-ciliated epithelia produce large, variable numbers of centrioles prior to ciliogenesis.
source: In contrast to cycling cells, in post-mitotic cells such as multi-ciliated epithelia, the genes required for centriole assembly are highly up-regulated (Hoh et al., 2012) to produce large, variable numbers of centrioles prior to ciliogenesis, a process thought to primarily depend on de novo assembly (Dirksen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Centriole production in multi-ciliated epithelia was thought to primarily depend on de novo assembly.
source: In contrast to cycling cells, in post-mitotic cells such as multi-ciliated epithelia, the genes required for centriole assembly are highly up-regulated (Hoh et al., 2012) to produce large, variable numbers of centrioles prior to ciliogenesis, a process thought to primarily depend on de novo assembly (Dirksen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The production of high quantities of centrioles in mouse multi-ciliated epithelia is driven by the pre-existing centriole rather than through de novo assembly.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that the production of high quantities of centrioles in mouse multi-ciliated epithelia is in fact driven by the pre-existing centriole rather than through de novo assembly (Al Jord et al., 2014), suggesting that the presence of pre-existing centrioles may have additional roles other than the number control for centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The presence of pre-existing centrioles may have additional roles other than number control for centriole biogenesis.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that the production of high quantities of centrioles in mouse multi-ciliated epithelia is in fact driven by the pre-existing centriole rather than through de novo assembly (Al Jord et al., 2014), suggesting that the presence of pre-existing centrioles may have additional roles other than the number control for centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited observation about centriole production in multi-ciliated epithelia.

claim: Centriole biogenesis starts with cartwheel assembly.
source: Centriole biogenesis, canonical or de novo, starts with cartwheel assembly, a geometric scaffold that defines the shape and structural integrity of centrioles (Anderson and Brenner, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The cartwheel is a geometric scaffold that defines the shape and structural integrity of centrioles.
source: Centriole biogenesis, canonical or de novo, starts with cartwheel assembly, a geometric scaffold that defines the shape and structural integrity of centrioles (Anderson and Brenner, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The backbone of the cartwheel is characterized by a central hub from which nine spokes emanate.
source: The backbone of the cartwheel is characterized by a central hub from which nine spokes emanate (Anderson and Brenner, 1971) and is primarily made of the centriolar protein SAS-6 (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cartwheel is primarily made of the centriolar protein SAS-6.
source: The backbone of the cartwheel is characterized by a central hub from which nine spokes emanate (Anderson and Brenner, 1971) and is primarily made of the centriolar protein SAS-6 (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SAS-6 exists as dimers which can self-oligomerize in vitro via an N-terminal head domain.
source: SAS-6 exists as dimers, which can self-oligomerize in vitro via an N-terminal head domain, forming a ring resembling the central hub, and C-terminal tails pointing outwards as spokes (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2014), albeit not always ninefold symmetric in vitro(Cottee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SAS-6 self-oligomerization forms a ring resembling the central hub with C-terminal tails pointing outwards as spokes.
source: SAS-6 exists as dimers, which can self-oligomerize in vitro via an N-terminal head domain, forming a ring resembling the central hub, and C-terminal tails pointing outwards as spokes (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2014), albeit not always ninefold symmetric in vitro(Cottee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SAS-6 self-oligomerization is not always ninefold symmetric in vitro.
source: SAS-6 exists as dimers, which can self-oligomerize in vitro via an N-terminal head domain, forming a ring resembling the central hub, and C-terminal tails pointing outwards as spokes (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2014), albeit not always ninefold symmetric in vitro(Cottee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A template-based assembly model dependent on the interaction of the C-terminal tail of SAS-6 with the lumen of mother centrioles has been proposed to initiate canonical duplication.
source: In contrast to the SAS-6 self-assembly model, a template-based assembly model, dependent on the interaction of the C-terminal tail of SAS-6 with the lumen of mother centrioles, has recently been proposed to initiate canonical duplication (Fong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During S phase, SAS-6 molecules are first recruited to the proximal lumen of the mother centriole prior to centriole duplication.
source: During S phase, SAS-6 molecules are first recruited to the proximal lumen of the mother centriole prior to centriole duplication, adopting a cartwheel-like organization through interactions with the luminal wall, rather than via their self-oligomerization activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Fong et al., 2014).

claim: SAS-6 adopts a cartwheel-like organization through interactions with the luminal wall, rather than via self-oligomerization activity.
source: During S phase, SAS-6 molecules are first recruited to the proximal lumen of the mother centriole prior to centriole duplication, adopting a cartwheel-like organization through interactions with the luminal wall, rather than via their self-oligomerization activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Fong et al., 2014).

claim: Mother centrioles may function as the template to shape SAS-6 assembly.
source: This leads to a proposal that mother centrioles may function as the template to shape SAS-6 assembly, thereby preserving the geometric shape of the centriole that otherwise cannot be ensured by SAS-6 self-assembly alone.
evidence: This is a proposal inferred from the template-based model.

claim: The geometric shape of the centriole cannot be ensured by SAS-6 self-assembly alone.
source: This leads to a proposal that mother centrioles may function as the template to shape SAS-6 assembly, thereby preserving the geometric shape of the centriole that otherwise cannot be ensured by SAS-6 self-assembly alone.
evidence: This is a proposal inferred from the template-based model.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 gene targeting was used to sequentially inactivate p53 and SAS-6 genes in RPE1 cells.
source: To characterize de novo formation of centrioles or centrosomes, we used CRISPR/Cas9 gene targeting to sequentially inactivate p53 and SAS-6 genes in retinal pigment epithelial cells (RPE1), generating stable, acentriolar cell lines (SAS-6-/-; p53-/-) in which de novo centrosome formation can be subsequently reconstituted (Izquierdo et al., 2014) (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Stable, acentriolar cell lines (SAS-6-/-; p53-/-) were generated in which de novo centrosome formation can be subsequently reconstituted.
source: To characterize de novo formation of centrioles or centrosomes, we used CRISPR/Cas9 gene targeting to sequentially inactivate p53 and SAS-6 genes in retinal pigment epithelial cells (RPE1), generating stable, acentriolar cell lines (SAS-6-/-; p53-/-) in which de novo centrosome formation can be subsequently reconstituted (Izquierdo et al., 2014) (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental result.

claim: Pure acentriolar cell lines were established through clonal propagation from single cells, a process taking 4–5 weeks.
source: Pure acentriolar cell lines were established through clonal propagation from single cells, a process taking 4–5 weeks, before these cells were used for experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Frameshift mutations present in the beginning of the coding region were found in each SAS-6 allele in clone #1 and #2.
source: In two independent SAS-6-/-; p53-/- cell lines we generated (clone #1 and #2), frameshift mutations present in the beginning of the coding region were found in each SAS-6 allele (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), predicting to produce severely truncated products consisting of 19 or 23 amino acids in clone #1 or #2, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The frameshift mutations in SAS-6 predict to produce severely truncated products consisting of 19 or 23 amino acids in clone #1 or #2, respectively.
source: In two independent SAS-6-/-; p53-/- cell lines we generated (clone #1 and #2), frameshift mutations present in the beginning of the coding region were found in each SAS-6 allele (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), predicting to produce severely truncated products consisting of 19 or 23 amino acids in clone #1 or #2, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data.

claim: Western blot analyses using antibodies against either the N- or C-terminal region of SAS-6 failed to detect any SAS-6 signal in SAS-6-/- cells.
source: Consistently, Western blot analyses using antibodies against either the N- or C-terminal region of SAS-6 failed to detect any SAS-6 signal in these cells (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Frameshift mutations were seen in TP53 alleles leading to loss of p53 function.
source: Similar frameshift mutations were also seen in TP53 alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), leading to loss of p53 function (Izquierdo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and citation.

claim: Both SAS-6 knockout cell lines completely lack centrioles or centrosomes.
source: Importantly, both SAS-6 knockout cell lines completely lack centrioles or centrosomes as expected (Figure 1A for clone #1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A for clone #2), but can continue to proliferate in the absence of p53 (Figure 1C for clone #1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B for clone #2) (Bazzi and Anderson, 2014; Izquierdo et al., 2014; Lambrus et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015), although their M phase is significantly lengthened (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SAS-6-/- cells can continue to proliferate in the absence of p53.
source: Importantly, both SAS-6 knockout cell lines completely lack centrioles or centrosomes as expected (Figure 1A for clone #1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A for clone #2), but can continue to proliferate in the absence of p53 (Figure 1C for clone #1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B for clone #2) (Bazzi and Anderson, 2014; Izquierdo et al., 2014; Lambrus et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015), although their M phase is significantly lengthened (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and citations.

claim: The M phase of SAS-6-/- cells is significantly lengthened.
source: Importantly, both SAS-6 knockout cell lines completely lack centrioles or centrosomes as expected (Figure 1A for clone #1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A for clone #2), but can continue to proliferate in the absence of p53 (Figure 1C for clone #1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B for clone #2) (Bazzi and Anderson, 2014; Izquierdo et al., 2014; Lambrus et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015), although their M phase is significantly lengthened (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: When exogenous wild-type, full length SAS-6 (SAS-6FL) was inducibly expressed in SAS-6-/- cells, variable numbers of centrosomes formed robustly in the absence of pre-existing centrosomes.
source: Intriguingly, when exogenous wild-type, full length SAS-6 (SAS-6FL) was inducibly expressed in SAS-6-/- cells (see 'Materials and methods' for details), either in clone #1 or #2, variable numbers of centrosomes formed robustly in the absence of pre-existing centrosomes (Figure 1E,G for clone #1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D for clone #2), a result consistent with previous reports (Lambrus et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: All SAS-6 fragments lacking the C-terminal domain (DM1, DM3, and DM5) failed to induce any centrosome formation.
source: All SAS-6 fragments lacking the C-terminal domain (DM1, DM3, and DM5) failed to induce any centrosome formation (Figure 1E,G), although expressed at similar or higher levels (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figures 1E, 1F, 1G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The C-terminal tail alone (DM6) was insufficient to induce centrosome formation.
source: The C-terminal tail alone (DM6) was also insufficient.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E,G.

claim: When the full-length coiled-coil domain (DM2) or a small portion of it (DM4) was present together with the C-terminal tail, it effectively drove de novo centrosome formation in all cells.
source: However, when the full-length coiled-coil domain (DM2) or a small portion of it (DM4) was present together with the C-terminal tail, it effectively drove de novo centrosome formation in all cells (Figure 1E,G; 100).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E,G.

claim: SAS-6 harboring the F131E mutation efficiently drove de novo centrosome formation (100%).
source: Consistently, SAS-6 harboring the F131E mutation (F131E) that has been previously shown to disrupt the oligomerization property of SAS-6 (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011) also efficiently drove de novo centrosome formation (Figure 1E–G,100%), with an expression level slightly higher than the endogenous level (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figures 1E, 1F, 1G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The F131E mutation has been previously shown to disrupt the oligomerization property of SAS-6.
source: Consistently, SAS-6 harboring the F131E mutation (F131E) that has been previously shown to disrupt the oligomerization property of SAS-6 (Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011) also efficiently drove de novo centrosome formation (Figure 1E–G,100%), with an expression level slightly higher than the endogenous level (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The fly SAS6 mutant equivalent to human SAS-6F131E could support the formation of some centriole-like structures in vivo.
source: A recent report showed that the fly SAS6 mutant equivalent to human SAS-6F131E could support the formation of some centriole-like structures in vivo (Cottee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The main activity of SAS-6 in promoting centriole assembly is possessed by its C-terminal portion, rather than the N-terminal domain mediating SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
source: Our result thus suggests that in contrary to the SAS-6 self-assembly model, the main activity of SAS-6 in promoting centriole assembly is possessed by its C-terminal portion, rather than the N-terminal domain mediating SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that C-terminal fragments can drive centriole formation.

claim: FL, F131E, DM2, and DM4 efficiently induced the formation of de novo centrioles in all cells (100%).
source: Consistently, FL, F131E, DM2, and DM4, all of which contain intact C-termini, efficiently induced the formation of de novo centrioles in all cells (100%), as revealed by the co-localization of centrin, SAS-6, STIL, CEP135, and CPAP (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some de novo centrioles formed with DM4 could mature properly by acquiring distal appendages.
source: Moreover, some of these de novo centrioles, even those formed with DM4 that lacks the entire N-terminal half of SAS-6, could later mature properly by acquiring distal appendages.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upon G1 arrest, some mature de novo centrioles were able to support ciliogenesis.
source: Importantly, upon G1 arrest, some of these mature centrioles were able to support ciliogenesis (Figure 2B), suggesting that functionally normal centrioles can arise from de novo assembly through SAS-6 mutants that are incapable of self-oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Functionally normal centrioles can arise from de novo assembly through SAS-6 mutants that are incapable of self-oligomerization.
source: Importantly, upon G1 arrest, some of these mature centrioles were able to support ciliogenesis (Figure 2B), suggesting that functionally normal centrioles can arise from de novo assembly through SAS-6 mutants that are incapable of self-oligomerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DM4-derived centrioles can ciliate.

claim: F131E- and DM4-derived centrioles could duplicate, with an efficiency grossly similar to or only slightly less than that of centrioles derived from wild-type SAS-6.
source: Strikingly, both F131E- and DM4-derived centrioles could duplicate, as revealed by centrin and STIL staining, with an efficiency grossly similar to or only slightly less than that of centrioles derived from wild-type SAS-6 (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Neither F131E nor DM4 could fully support centriole duplication in previous reports.
source: This result, however, appears inconsistent with previous reports, where neither F131E nor DM4 could fully support centriole duplication (Fong et al., 2014; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011), although both were able to initiate SAS-6/cartwheel assembly in the presence of pre-existing centrioles (Fong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: F131E and DM4 were able to initiate SAS-6/cartwheel assembly in the presence of pre-existing centrioles.
source: This result, however, appears inconsistent with previous reports, where neither F131E nor DM4 could fully support centriole duplication (Fong et al., 2014; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011), although both were able to initiate SAS-6/cartwheel assembly in the presence of pre-existing centrioles (Fong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: F131E or DM4 can support the duplication of F131E- or DM4-derived centrioles, respectively, but not pre-existing, wild-type SAS-6-derived centrioles.
source: We do not understand the reason behind this discrepancy, but the result that F131E or DM4 can support the duplication of F131E- or DM4-derived centrioles, respectively (Figure 2C,D), but not pre-existing, wild-type SAS-6-derived centrioles (Fong et al., 2014; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011) raises an idea that perhaps pre-existing centrioles have an active, dominant role in guiding canonical duplication.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D and citations to previous work.

claim: Pre-existing centrioles may have an active, dominant role in guiding canonical duplication.
source: We do not understand the reason behind this discrepancy, but the result that F131E or DM4 can support the duplication of F131E- or DM4-derived centrioles, respectively (Figure 2C,D), but not pre-existing, wild-type SAS-6-derived centrioles (Fong et al., 2014; Kitagawa et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2011) raises an idea that perhaps pre-existing centrioles have an active, dominant role in guiding canonical duplication.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior of mutant SAS-6 with de novo versus pre-existing centrioles.

claim: Normal looking centrioles could be easily found in cells expressing either F131E or DM4.
source: To our surprise, normal looking centrioles, which are characterized as 200 nm x 500 nm in size, made of nine microtubule triplets, and equipped with distal and sub-distal appendages, could be easily found in cells expressing either F131E or DM4 (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: EM tomography reconstruction of a centriole from DM4 expressing cells revealed a perfect ninefold symmetric shape.
source: In particular, EM tomography reconstruction of a centriole from DM4 expressing cells revealed a perfect ninefold symmetric shape (Figure 3B; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by EM tomography data shown in Figure 3B and Video 1.

claim: At least some DM4-derived centrioles could ciliate.
source: Moreover, EM analyses also confirmed that at least some DM4-derived centrioles could ciliate (Figure 3C) and duplicate (Figure 3D), firmly demonstrating that neither structural assembly nor shape determination of centrioles strictly depends on the self-oligomerization activity of SAS-6.
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At least some DM4-derived centrioles could duplicate.
source: Moreover, EM analyses also confirmed that at least some DM4-derived centrioles could ciliate (Figure 3C) and duplicate (Figure 3D), firmly demonstrating that neither structural assembly nor shape determination of centrioles strictly depends on the self-oligomerization activity of SAS-6.
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Neither structural assembly nor shape determination of centrioles strictly depends on the self-oligomerization activity of SAS-6.
source: Moreover, EM analyses also confirmed that at least some DM4-derived centrioles could ciliate (Figure 3C) and duplicate (Figure 3D), firmly demonstrating that neither structural assembly nor shape determination of centrioles strictly depends on the self-oligomerization activity of SAS-6.
evidence: This is inferred from the EM data showing normal centrioles formed with DM4.

claim: The C-terminal half of SAS-6 is both required and sufficient for centriole biogenesis.
source: Rather, the C-terminal half of SAS-6 is both required and sufficient for centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that C-terminal fragments can drive centriole formation.

claim: Canonically duplicated centrioles are essentially free of error in their size, structural integrity, and geometric shape (100%, n = 70).
source: EM analyses revealed that canonically duplicated centrioles are essentially free of error in their size, structural integrity, and geometric shape (Figure 4E, 100%, n = 70).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A small but significant portion of de novo centrioles are abnormal, including centrioles missing variable numbers of MT triplets, or varying in size or shape.
source: In striking contrast, we consistently observed a small but significant portion of de novo centrioles that are abnormal, including centrioles missing variable numbers of MT triplets, or varying in size or shape (Figure 4A–D; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4A–D and Video 2.

claim: Similar types of abnormalities were seen regardless of whether centrioles were derived from SAS-6FL, SAS-6F131E, or SAS-6DM4.
source: Importantly, similar types of abnormalities were seen regardless of whether centrioles were derived from SAS-6FL, SAS-6F131E, or SAS-6DM4.
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Abnormally looking de novo centrioles appeared to have normal activities.
source: Nevertheless, these abnormally looking centrioles appeared to have normal activities, suggesting that they are not simply unstable structures in the process of non-specific disintegration.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of abnormal centrioles that can duplicate or mature.

claim: SAS-6FL-derived centrioles that had only six MT triplets were able to duplicate, producing daughter centrioles also made of an incomplete set of MT triplets.
source: For example, we observed SAS-6FL-derived centrioles that had only six MT triplets, but able to duplicate, producing daughter centrioles also made of an incomplete set of MT triplets (Figure 4A-#1).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4A-#1.

claim: SAS-6FL-derived centrioles that appeared larger than normal centrioles were able to mature and acquire appendages.
source: SAS-6FL-derived centrioles that appeared larger than normal centrioles (Figure 4A-#2), but able to mature and acquire appendages were also found.
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4A-#2.

claim: The width (outer diameter) of SAS-6FL-derived centrioles is more variable than that of canonically duplicated centrioles.
source: Consequently, the width (outer diameter) of SAS-6FL-derived centrioles is more variable than that of canonically duplicated centrioles (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: De novo centrioles made of disorganized, or abnormal numbers of, MT triplets have been seen to form in cells depleted of the endogenous centrioles by laser ablation.
source: De novo centrioles made of disorganized, or abnormal numbers of, MT triplets have also been seen to form in cells depleted of the endogenous centrioles by laser ablation (La Terra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DM4-mediated de novo synthesis has an error rate higher than those mediated by SAS-6FL.
source: Notably, DM4-mediated, but not F131E-mediated, de novo synthesis clearly has an error rate higher than those mediated by SAS-6FL (Figure 4E), suggesting that the N-terminal half of SAS-6 is involved in some additional processes that ensure the accuracy or quality control of centriole assembly.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The N-terminal half of SAS-6 is involved in some additional processes that ensure the accuracy or quality control of centriole assembly.
source: Notably, DM4-mediated, but not F131E-mediated, de novo synthesis clearly has an error rate higher than those mediated by SAS-6FL (Figure 4E), suggesting that the N-terminal half of SAS-6 is involved in some additional processes that ensure the accuracy or quality control of centriole assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DM4 has a higher error rate than FL.

claim: In the absence of pre-existing centrioles, de novo centriole synthesis can occur, largely independent of SAS-6 self-oligomerization.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that in the absence of pre-existing centrioles, de novo centriole synthesis can occur, largely independent of SAS-6 self-oligomerization, but the process is inherently error-prone, and may require the presence of pre-existing centrioles to achieve high accuracy.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: De novo centriole synthesis is inherently error-prone.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that in the absence of pre-existing centrioles, de novo centriole synthesis can occur, largely independent of SAS-6 self-oligomerization, but the process is inherently error-prone, and may require the presence of pre-existing centrioles to achieve high accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by EM data showing structural defects in de novo centrioles.

claim: De novo centriole synthesis may require the presence of pre-existing centrioles to achieve high accuracy.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that in the absence of pre-existing centrioles, de novo centriole synthesis can occur, largely independent of SAS-6 self-oligomerization, but the process is inherently error-prone, and may require the presence of pre-existing centrioles to achieve high accuracy.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of error rates between de novo and canonical duplication.

claim: Self-oligomerization of SAS-6 is not essential for the structural assembly or shape determination of centrioles.
source: Using this system, we found that self-oligomerization of SAS-6, an activity proposed to drive cartwheel/centriole formation, is in fact not essential for the structural assembly or shape determination of centrioles.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing normal centrioles formed without SAS-6 self-oligomerization.

claim: De novo centriole formation can be sufficiently driven by the C-terminal half of SAS-6 lacking the self-oligomerization activity.
source: Instead, de novo centriole formation can be sufficiently driven by the C-terminal half of SAS-6 lacking the self-oligomerization activity, fundamentally deviating from the current paradigm for centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing DM4 can drive centriole formation.

claim: In human cells, de novo centriole assembly is an error-prone process that generates abnormal centrioles in a significantly higher frequency comparing to canonical duplication.
source: Moreover, our results show that in human cells, de novo centriole assembly is an error-prone process that generates abnormal centrioles in a significantly higher frequency comparing to canonical duplication.
evidence: This is supported by EM data showing higher error rates in de novo centrioles.

claim: The error rate of de novo assembly could potentially be underestimated, as it is plausible that the de novo centrioles formed initially are actually much more error-prone.
source: The error rate of de novo assembly, which was estimated from later stages of centrioles, could potentially be underestimated, as it is plausible that the de novo centrioles formed initially are actually much more error-prone, and that over time ninefold symmetric centrioles persist because they are more stable or more efficient to duplicate.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential selection bias in the observed centrioles.

claim: Over time ninefold symmetric centrioles may persist because they are more stable or more efficient to duplicate.
source: The error rate of de novo assembly, which was estimated from later stages of centrioles, could potentially be underestimated, as it is plausible that the de novo centrioles formed initially are actually much more error-prone, and that over time ninefold symmetric centrioles persist because they are more stable or more efficient to duplicate.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about why normal centrioles might be observed more frequently.

claim: If de novo assembly must be used for centriole production, the structural accuracy may need to be insured or reinforced by other mechanisms.
source: In any case, our results suggest that if de novo assembly must be used for centriole production, the structural accuracy may need to be insured or reinforced by other mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that de novo assembly is error-prone.

claim: The expression level of the SAS-6FL or SAS-6F131E in the cell-based assay is higher than the endogenous level of SAS-6 responsible for canonical duplication.
source: The expression level of the SAS-6FL or SAS-6F131E in our cell-based assay is higher than the endogenous level of SAS-6 responsible for canonical duplication (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), a condition that may potentially affect the accuracy of de novo centriole assembly.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: De novo centriole assembly is normally blocked under physiological conditions for number control.
source: However, as de novo centriole assembly is normally blocked under physiological conditions (for number control), it is unclear what the 'right' level of SAS-6 should be, or if the level really matters that much, when the number control is not a relevant issue for de novo assembly.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about centriole number control.

claim: De novo centrioles made of disorganized, or abnormal numbers of MT blades are formed with the endogenous level of SAS-6.
source: Consistently, it has been reported that de novo centrioles made of disorganized, or abnormal numbers of MT blades are formed with the endogenous level of SAS-6 (La Terra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During multiciliogenesis, SAS-6 level is highly up-regulated and almost every new centriole forms correctly.
source: Conversely, during multiciliogenesis where SAS-6 level is highly up-regulated (Hoh et al., 2012), almost every new centriole forms correctly.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When cells carry pre-existing centrioles, they could perhaps tolerate a wider range of SAS-6 level for proper structural assembly of centrioles.
source: These results suggest that when cells carry pre-existing centrioles, they could perhaps tolerate a wider range of SAS-6 level for proper structural assembly of centrioles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations about SAS-6 levels and centriole formation accuracy.

claim: Numerical control of centriole biogenesis is highly sensitive to the sas-6 level, even in the presence of pre-existing centrioles.
source: Numerical control of centriole biogenesis, however, is a different issue, as it is highly sensitive to the sas-6 level (Strnad et al., 2007), even in the presence of pre-existing centrioles.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Large quantities of centrioles naturally arising from the acentriolar pathway has been reported in planarians.
source: Large quantities of centrioles naturally arising from the acentriolar pathway has been reported in planarians (Azimzadeh et al., 2012), but whether the same process occurs in vertebrates under normal physiological conditions is unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Whether de novo centriole synthesis occurs in vertebrates under normal physiological conditions is unclear.
source: Large quantities of centrioles naturally arising from the acentriolar pathway has been reported in planarians (Azimzadeh et al., 2012), but whether the same process occurs in vertebrates under normal physiological conditions is unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: In vertebrate somatic cycling cells, the birth of a new centriole is normally given by the pre-existing centriole (canonical duplication).
source: In vertebrate somatic cycling cells, the birth of a new centriole is normally given by the pre-existing centriole (canonical duplication), a process known to regulate the number at which newborn centrioles can form.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about centriole biology.

claim: Canonical duplication is a process known to regulate the number at which newborn centrioles can form.
source: In vertebrate somatic cycling cells, the birth of a new centriole is normally given by the pre-existing centriole (canonical duplication), a process known to regulate the number at which newborn centrioles can form.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about centriole biology.

claim: In multi-ciliated epithelia, de novo assembly is not responsible for the production of hundreds of centrioles.
source: Strikingly, a recent report showed that in multi-ciliated epithelia, de novo assembly is not responsible for the production of hundreds of centrioles (Al Jord et al., 2014); instead, all new centrioles that later form cilia are initiated, directly or indirectly, from the pre-existing centriole, supporting the idea that the presence of pre-existing centrioles has additional roles other than the number control for centriole reproduction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In multi-ciliated epithelia, all new centrioles that later form cilia are initiated, directly or indirectly, from the pre-existing centriole.
source: Strikingly, a recent report showed that in multi-ciliated epithelia, de novo assembly is not responsible for the production of hundreds of centrioles (Al Jord et al., 2014); instead, all new centrioles that later form cilia are initiated, directly or indirectly, from the pre-existing centriole, supporting the idea that the presence of pre-existing centrioles has additional roles other than the number control for centriole reproduction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pre-existing centrioles can specify some steps of the assembly process that define the structural integrity of the centriole.
source: Our results that canonically duplicated centrioles are predominantly free of error, while de novo centriole assembly is error-prone, suggest that perhaps pre-existing centrioles can specify some steps of the assembly process that define the structural integrity of the centriole (e.g. cartwheel assembly), an idea consistent with the template-based model of centriole formation proposed recently (Fong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of error rates and is consistent with the template-based model.

claim: Mouse embryogenesis starts with a fertilized egg lacking apparent centrioles/centrosomes.
source: Notably, mouse embryos show exceptions that break all the known rules. The mouse embryogenesis starts with a fertilized egg lacking apparent centrioles/centrosomes, and finishes with an intact animal in which nearly all cells carry centrioles that are both numerically and structurally normal (Abumuslimov et al., 1994; Gueth-Hallonet et al., 1993; Howe and FitzHarris, 2013; Palacios et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mouse embryogenesis finishes with an intact animal in which nearly all cells carry centrioles that are both numerically and structurally normal.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: How acentrosomal cells in mouse embryos escape from p53 dependent elimination acting against acentrosomal mitosis is not understood.
source: How acentrosomal cells in mouse embryos escape from p53 dependent elimination acting against acentrosomal mitosis (Bazzi and Anderson, 2014; Lambrus et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015), and how they later form and maintain proper centrioles in the absence of pre-existing centrioles are completely not understood.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Other unanticipated mechanisms may be specifically involved in centriole biogenesis in early mouse embryos.
source: With our surprising observation that SAS-6 self-oligomerization is not essential for centriole assembly, perhaps other unanticipated mechanisms are specifically involved in centriole biogenesis in early mouse embryos.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study.
